title: Speeds and feeds for 6061 aluminum vs 4140 steel on a manual lathe
summary: Translate supplied cutting speeds into RPM, then distinguish feed from travel rate.

blocks.heading: Material name alone does not select a cutting speed
blocks.body: 6061 aluminum and 4140 steel are not complete setup descriptions. Establish temper or hardness, tool material and geometry, diameter, workholding, machine limits and the operation. The numbers below are supplied arithmetic examples, not recommended cutting settings.

blocks.heading: Two fictional 2 in diameter examples
rows: Assume approved by a tooling reference
Assume approved by a tooling reference
blocks.caption: RPM = 12 × SFM / (π × diameter in inches). These assumed speeds do not substitute for a tooling supplier’s data for your exact tool and material condition.

blocks.heading: Convert surface speed at the actual diameter
blocks.body: At 300 SFM and 2 in: RPM = 3.82 × 300 / 2 ≈ 573. At 100 SFM: RPM ≈ 191. A manual machine offers discrete speeds; choose a suitable available setting within the machine, chuck and workholding limits, then calculate the actual surface speed. Do not automatically round upward.

blocks.heading: Same supplied SFM, different diameters
blocks.caption: Doubling diameter halves the RPM for the same surface speed. A machine limit can make the target surface speed unavailable.

blocks.heading: The gearbox setting and the traverse rate are different
blocks.body: Feed in inches per revolution describes how far the tool advances for each spindle revolution. Multiply by RPM for inches per minute. At 573 RPM and 0.004 in/rev, travel is about 2.29 in/min. Reducing RPM reduces that travel rate even when the gearbox feed setting is unchanged.

blocks.heading: Radial depth is half the diameter change
blocks.body: Turning a diameter from 2.000 to 1.900 in removes 0.050 in radially. Treat depth, feed and speed as separate inputs. A speed calculation does not tell you whether a slender workpiece, a small machine or a particular insert can carry the planned cut.

blocks.heading: What the material comparison should make you check
rows: Confirm alloy/temper and tool guidance for adhesion and chip control
Confirm annealed, prehardened or other condition; hardness changes the job
Inspect built-up edge and surface condition
Inspect edge wear, cutting forces and tool suitability
Avoid assuming shiny chips mean a sound setup
Avoid assuming all 4140 behaves like soft bar stock
blocks.caption: These are inspection prompts, not a speed chart.

blocks.heading: Choose the correct RPM
blocks.prompt: A supplied cutting speed is 100 SFM and the diameter is 1 in. Approximately what RPM follows?
blocks.explanation: 3.82 × 100 / 1 = 382 RPM, before machine and setup limits.

blocks.heading: Read a diameter change
blocks.prompt: You turn 1.500 in stock to 1.400 in. What radial depth was removed?
blocks.explanation: The diameter fell by 0.100 in, so radial depth is half: 0.050 in.

blocks.heading: A usable setup note records all of this
items: Exact material and condition; tool designation and supplier’s recommended range.
Starting diameter, planned final diameter and workholding arrangement.
Chosen machine RPM, feed per revolution and radial depth.
A stopped-spindle inspection plan for size, finish, chip control and tool condition.
What observation would stop the cut or prompt a documented adjustment.

blocks.heading: Why the centre behaves differently
blocks.body: At fixed RPM during facing, surface speed falls as the tool approaches the centre. A CNC constant-surface-speed mode can compensate within limits; a manual lathe usually cannot do this automatically. Never borrow a CNC mode assumption for a manual-machine setup.

items.label: Sandvik Coromant: general turning formulas
items.detail: Definitions of cutting speed, spindle speed, feed and depth. All numerical setups on this page are fictional arithmetic exercises.
